concepts.title: The First Empire
concepts.contentHtml:
The Qin dynasty (221-206 BCE) unified China for the first time under Qin Shi Huang, who standardized writing, measurements, currency, and the legal code. He also built the first version of the Great Wall and was buried with the Terracotta Army.

The Han dynasty (206 BCE-220 CE) consolidated and expanded. Confucianism became the state ideology. The Silk Road opened to the west. Han influence was so deep that ethnic Chinese still call themselves 'Han'.

concepts.title: Tang and Song
concepts.contentHtml:
The Tang dynasty (618-907) is often called China's golden age. Cosmopolitan, prosperous, with Chang'an the world's largest city. Buddhism flourished alongside Confucianism. Poetry of Li Bai and Du Fu defined classical Chinese literature.

The Song dynasty (960-1279) saw economic and technological brilliance: paper money, gunpowder, movable-type printing, magnetic compass for navigation, advanced metallurgy. By some economic measures Song China surpassed contemporary Europe.

concepts.title: Ming and Qing
concepts.contentHtml:
After Mongol Yuan dynasty (1271-1368), the Ming (1368-1644) restored Han Chinese rule. Zheng He's massive treasure fleets sailed to Africa, then voyages were halted. The Forbidden City was built; the Great Wall fortified.

The Qing (1644-1912) was Manchu — a non-Han conquest dynasty that nonetheless ruled in Chinese style. Population doubled to ~400 million. The 19th century brought catastrophic decline: opium wars, unequal treaties, Taiping Rebellion (~20 million dead), foreign concessions.

The 1911 revolution ended imperial China after over 2000 years of dynastic rule.

title: Japan
description: Island nation from samurai to Meiji to modern

concepts.title: Classical and Medieval Japan
concepts.contentHtml:
The Heian period (794-1185) refined Japanese court culture — Lady Murasaki's Tale of Genji, often called the world's first novel, dates to ~1000 CE. The Kamakura period (1185-1333) saw the rise of samurai warrior class and shogun military government.

The Tokugawa shogunate (1603-1868) imposed sakoku — closure to most foreign contact — for over 200 years. Internal peace, urban culture (Edo became the world's largest city by some 1700s measures), and refined arts (kabuki, ukiyo-e, tea ceremony) flourished.

concepts.title: Meiji Restoration
concepts.contentHtml:
Commodore Perry's American gunboats in 1853 forced Japan open. Recognizing the threat, Japan rapidly modernized in the Meiji Restoration (1868). In a generation, it transformed into an industrial power with constitutional government, conscript army, modern education.

Japan defeated Qing China (1894-95) and Russia (1904-05) — the first modern Asian state to defeat European powers. Korean colonization (1910), Taiwan (since 1895), and growing imperial ambitions followed.

concepts.title: Imperial Japan and Postwar
concepts.contentHtml:
Japan's invasion of Manchuria (1931) and full-scale war with China (1937) led into WWII. Pearl Harbor (December 1941) brought the US in. Atomic bombs at Hiroshima and Nagasaki (August 1945) ended the war.

Postwar Japan rebuilt under US occupation (1945-52). Constitution renounced war. Rapid economic growth made Japan the world's second-largest economy by 1968 — the 'Japanese economic miracle'.

The 1990s 'lost decade' followed an asset-bubble collapse. Japan today is wealthy but demographically aging, navigating tense relations with China and a rearming security environment.

concepts.title: Korean History
concepts.contentHtml:
Korea's Three Kingdoms period (Goguryeo, Baekje, Silla) ended with Silla's unification in 668. The Goryeo dynasty (918-1392) saw Buddhism flourish; the Joseon dynasty (1392-1897) was Confucian and developed hangul writing system under King Sejong (1443) — among the world's most rationally designed scripts.

Japanese annexation (1910-1945) was harsh. After WWII, the peninsula was divided at the 38th parallel — Soviet north, US south. The Korean War (1950-53) entrenched the division; technically the war never ended (armistice, not peace treaty).

South Korea's economic transformation since the 1960s — from poorer than Ghana to a developed economy and democracy — is one of modern history's most striking development stories.

concepts.title: Vietnam
concepts.contentHtml:
Vietnam was a Chinese province for ~1000 years (111 BCE - 938 CE). Independence afterwards saw alternating dynasties under Chinese cultural influence but separate political identity.

French colonization began in the 1850s, fully consolidated by 1887 as part of French Indochina. Independence movements grew, culminating in Ho Chi Minh's declaration of independence in 1945.

The First Indochina War (1946-54) ended with French defeat at Dien Bien Phu. Partition followed; the Vietnam War (~1955-75) drew in the US. North Vietnamese victory unified the country in 1976. Doi Moi reforms (1986) opened the economy. Vietnam today is among Asia's fastest-growing economies.

concepts.title: Cultural Sphere
concepts.contentHtml:
Korea, Vietnam, and Japan all historically used Chinese writing for scholarly and government purposes (similar to Latin in medieval Europe). All three developed unique additions or alternatives — kana in Japan, hangul in Korea, chữ nôm in Vietnam (later replaced by Latin-based quoc ngu).

Confucian values, Buddhist religion, and Chinese-style imperial administrative models spread across this 'Chinese cultural sphere' — though each country retained distinct identity.

Modern East Asia is economically integrated and culturally interconnected (K-pop, J-anime, Chinese cinema all cross borders), but political tensions among the four major nations remain.

title: Modern China
description: Republic, civil war, communist revolution, reform

concepts.title: Republic and Civil War
concepts.contentHtml:
After the 1911 revolution, the Republic of China struggled with warlords, Japanese encroachment, and a civil war between Chiang Kai-shek's Kuomintang (founded by Sun Yat-sen) and the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).

The Long March (1934-35) was a CCP retreat covering ~9000 km — Mao Zedong emerged as paramount leader. Japanese invasion (1937-1945) interrupted the civil war; both sides nominally cooperated against Japan.

Civil war resumed after WWII; the CCP won by 1949. Chiang's nationalists fled to Taiwan, where they ruled until democratic transitions in the late 20th century.

concepts.title: Mao's China
concepts.contentHtml:
The People's Republic was proclaimed in 1949. Land reform (~1-2 million landlords killed). Korean War. The Hundred Flowers Campaign (1956-57) briefly invited criticism, then crushed dissenters.

The Great Leap Forward (1958-62) tried to industrialize through collectivization. Catastrophic famine killed 15-45 million people — likely the deadliest famine in history.

The Cultural Revolution (1966-76) attacked 'old' culture, professional classes, and Mao's political enemies. Million+ deaths; vast cultural destruction. Mao's death in 1976 ended the era.

concepts.title: Reform and Rise
concepts.contentHtml:
Deng Xiaoping launched economic reforms from 1978 — special economic zones, opening to foreign investment, agricultural reform. The transformation since is among the most dramatic in human history. Hundreds of millions lifted out of poverty.

The Tiananmen Square massacre (1989) crushed pro-democracy protests; political reform stalled. Economic growth continued at extraordinary rates.

By the 2010s, China was the world's second-largest economy, second-largest military, and a rising geopolitical power. Xi Jinping's tenure has seen further authoritarian consolidation. China's 21st-century role remains a defining global question.

concepts.title: East Asian Cultural Export
concepts.contentHtml:
K-pop, K-drama, Korean cinema (Bong Joon-ho's Parasite won Best Picture in 2020). Japanese anime and manga have global followings. Chinese cinema, literature, and cuisine are increasingly visible internationally.

Asian-Pacific export of cultural goods is among the largest on Earth. The 'Korean Wave' (Hallyu) is now a multi-billion-dollar industry. East Asia's cultural reach in the 21st century rivals Hollywood's.

concepts.title: Demographic Crisis
concepts.contentHtml:
East Asia's strikingly low birthrates threaten its long-term position. South Korea's TFR is below 1.0 — among the lowest ever recorded. Japan, Taiwan, Hong Kong, and increasingly mainland China are all in deep below-replacement territory.

Aging populations pressure pension systems and labor markets. Japan has been the early case study; China is following with the additional complication of decades of one-child policy.

Immigration is politically constrained in most East Asian countries; automation and immigration of women into the workforce help but only partly.

concepts.title: 21st-Century Geopolitics
concepts.contentHtml:
US-China rivalry defines much of 21st-century global politics. Trade tensions, technology decoupling, military competition, especially over Taiwan.

Japan and South Korea are democratic US allies. North Korea remains a nuclear-armed totalitarian state. Taiwan's status is contested — Chinese unification claims meet Taiwanese identity.

How East Asia evolves over the next decades — peaceful competition, cold war, or hot war — will shape the world. The region holds about a third of global GDP and most of the supply chains for advanced technology.
